cls: Opioid analgesic - synthetic phenylpiperidine mu-opioid receptor agonist
pharm: Synthetic opioid agonist acting at mu-opioid receptors to produce analgesia and sedation; shorter-acting than morphine with an active, neurotoxic metabolite (normeperidine) that can accumulate and cause seizures, especially in renal impairment.

Oral may be taken with or without food; with food if nausea

Reduce dose; impaired metabolism prolongs effect

summary: Pethidine (meperidine) is a synthetic phenylpiperidine opioid agonist used for the management of moderate to severe acute pain when an opioid is appropriate and alternative treatments are inadequate, and as an adjunct to anesthesia and for obstetric analgesia. Acting at mu-opioid receptors, it produces analgesia, sedation, and euphoria along with respiratory depression. It is a Schedule II controlled substance and is habit-forming, with risks of abuse, addiction, misuse, and life-threatening respiratory depression. A key limitation is its active metabolite normeperidine, which is neurotoxic and accumulates with repeated dosing, renal impairment, or high doses, causing tremor, myoclonus, agitation, and seizures - so it is not recommended for chronic pain and should be avoided in renal impairment and the elderly. Because of a dangerous interaction with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (severe serotonin toxicity, hyperthermia, and cardiovascular instability), pethidine is contraindicated with MAOIs and within 14 days of their use. It interacts with alcohol and other CNS depressants to cause additive, potentially fatal respiratory depression and sedation. Largely superseded by morphine and other opioids for routine use.
indications: Management of moderate to severe acute pain when use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate and alternatives are inadequate
Analgesia during labor and delivery (obstetric pain)
Preoperative medication and support of anesthesia / adjunct to anesthesia

Adjust for age and physical status

Slow intravenous injection (when used IV) must be given very slowly and diluted; have resuscitation equipment and naloxone available

moa: Pethidine (meperidine) is a synthetic opioid that acts as an agonist primarily at mu (and to a lesser extent kappa) opioid receptors in the central nervous system. Activation of these G-protein-coupled receptors inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reduces neuronal excitability and neurotransmitter release, and alters the perception of and emotional response to pain, producing analgesia, sedation, and euphoria. Opioid agonism in the brainstem respiratory centers reduces sensitivity to carbon dioxide, causing dose-dependent respiratory depression. Pethidine also has mild anticholinergic and local anesthetic properties and inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, which contributes to its risk of serotonin toxicity with serotonergic drugs and MAO inhibitors. It is metabolized in the liver to normeperidine, an active metabolite with reduced analgesic activity but central nervous system excitatory (proconvulsant) effects that accumulate when clearance is impaired.

absolute: Current use of, or use within the last 14 days of, monoamine oxidase inhibitors (risk of severe, potentially fatal serotonin toxicity/reaction)
Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction, including paralytic ileus
relative: Renal impairment (normeperidine accumulation and seizures - avoid)
Hepatic impairment and the elderly/debilitated (reduce dose)
Head injury, raised intracranial pressure, or impaired consciousness
Concomitant alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants; concomitant serotonergic drugs
History of substance use disorder; pregnancy and labor (neonatal effects)
monitor: Respiratory rate, depth, and oxygen saturation
Level of sedation and mental status
Central nervous system excitation - tremor, myoclonus, agitation, seizures (normeperidine toxicity)
Signs of misuse, abuse, dependence, and serotonin syndrome

preg: Pethidine crosses the placenta. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. When used during labor it can cause respiratory depression and behavioral changes in the newborn; prolonged use in pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Have neonatal resuscitation and naloxone available at delivery.
lact: Pethidine and its metabolite normeperidine are excreted into breast milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding; monitor the infant for drowsiness, poor feeding, and respiratory depression. Because of the active metabolite, repeated maternal dosing may lead to accumulation in the breastfed infant.
renal: Avoid pethidine in patients with renal impairment. The active metabolite normeperidine is renally eliminated and accumulates when renal function is reduced, increasing the risk of central nervous system excitation, tremor, myoclonus, and seizures. If an opioid is required, choose an alternative agent.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment reduces metabolism of pethidine, prolonging and intensifying its effects and increasing sensitivity. Reduce the dose, lengthen the dosing interval, and monitor closely; avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (current or within 14 days) - life-threatening serotonin/opioid toxicity (hyperthermia, rigidity, seizures, cardiovascular instability); CONTRAINDICATED

Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants (including alcohol, sedatives, other opioids) - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death; avoid or use with extreme caution at reduced doses
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, linezolid, tramadol) - risk of serotonin syndrome
moderate: CYP3A4/CYP2B6 inhibitors and inducers - alter pethidine and normeperidine levels (toxicity or reduced effect/withdrawal)
Mixed agonist-antagonist or partial agonist opioids (e.g., buprenorphine, nalbuphine) - may reduce analgesia and precipitate withdrawal
Anticholinergic drugs - additive risk of urinary retention and constipation/ileus
Antihypertensives and diuretics - enhanced hypotensive effect
minor: Phenytoin and other enzyme inducers can increase normeperidine formation
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food (oral); take with food if nausea occurs.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive central nervous system and respiratory depression that can be fatal.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum amylase and lipase (spasm of the sphincter of Oddi); can produce positive opioid results on urine drug screens.

serious: Central nervous system excitation - tremor, myoclonus, agitation, and seizures (normeperidine toxicity)
emergency: Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing or marked drowsiness/unresponsiveness (overdose)
High fever, agitation, rigidity, rapid heart rate (serotonin syndrome - especially after MAOI)

monitoring: Respiratory rate, depth, and oxygen saturation, especially after the first dose and dose increases
Sedation level, mental status, and signs of CNS excitation (tremor, myoclonus, seizures)
Pain control and analgesic effectiveness; avoid use beyond short-term acute pain
Signs of misuse, abuse, dependence, and withdrawal; bowel function for constipation
counsel: This is a strong opioid painkiller and a controlled medicine - take it exactly as prescribed, only for short-term pain, and never share it
Do not drink alcohol or take sedatives/sleeping tablets with it; the combination can dangerously slow or stop your breathing
Tell your doctor about all medicines, especially any antidepressants or 'MAOI' medicines, which can cause a serious reaction with this drug
It can cause drowsiness and dizziness - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Report muscle twitching, shakiness, confusion, or any fit/seizure straight away
Get emergency help for very slow or difficult breathing or extreme sleepiness; keep the medicine away from children, as it is habit-forming
pk: Peak analgesic effect ~1 hour after injection
Pethidine ~3-5 hours; normeperidine ~15-30 hours (longer in renal failure)
Analgesia lasts approximately 2-4 hours (shorter than morphine)
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light; secure as a controlled substance
pearls: Habit forming: Yes - Schedule II controlled substance with high abuse and dependence potential
Active metabolite normeperidine is neurotoxic/proconvulsant and accumulates with repeated dosing or renal impairment - AVOID in renal impairment, in the elderly, and for chronic pain
Contraindicated with MAO inhibitors and within 14 days of stopping them - can cause fatal serotonin toxicity, hyperthermia, and cardiovascular collapse
Avoid combining with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants - additive, potentially fatal respiratory depression
Shorter duration than morphine (~2-4 h); naloxone reverses respiratory depression but does NOT reverse normeperidine-induced seizures (treat seizures with benzodiazepines, not naloxone)
Largely superseded by morphine and other opioids; reserve for short-term acute pain only and use the lowest effective dose
missed: Pethidine is usually given as needed for pain rather than on a fixed schedule. If it is prescribed at set times and a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose - do not double up. Do not take extra doses to catch up.
overdose: Overdose causes respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils (though pupils may be dilated with significant normeperidine accumulation or hypoxia), extreme drowsiness progressing to stupor or coma, skeletal muscle flaccidity, cold/clammy skin, hypotension, and potentially death. Normeperidine accumulation can cause seizures. Management: secure the airway and support ventilation, administer the opioid antagonist naloxone (repeated/infusion as needed because pethidine outlasts a single dose), give supportive care, and treat seizures with benzodiazepines - naloxone alone will not stop normeperidine-induced seizures.
